article_title: Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education
citation: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education.
title: CGScholar AI Helper: cloud-based AI writing feedback tool with rubric-guided, teacher-steerable feedback
description: The CGScholar AI Helper is a cloud-based web application supporting student writing through AI-driven feedback and iterative revision. It uses a split-screen interface with a multimodal text editor and a feedback area, a workflow of drafting, AI feedback, revision, optional peer review, reflection, and publication, and prompt engineering with multi-agent and chain-of-thought approaches. Retrieval-Augmented Generation 'prioritizes teacher-approved materials from the knowledge base over the foundation language models (LLMs) to ensure factually accurate feedback.' Teachers supply rubrics and knowledge bases; AI feedback appears one criterion at a time, and students can request clarifications.
requirements: Teachers provide an assessment rubric with criteria, rating levels, and descriptions, plus a knowledge base of relevant instructional materials
constraints: The study notes technical issues such as delays in feedback generation and occasional system errors, and that the tool's feedback vocabulary was challenging for some students
examples: In the Alaska case study, the tool was integrated into a journal writing activity on belonging, with a teacher-created rubric assessing topic clarity, supporting evidence, explanation, conclusion, formal tone, organization, and mechanics on a four-point scale.
key_sources: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/s8hqe_v1

article_title: CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm
citation: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3
title: CGRP neurons bias defensive response selection toward passive freezing under high threat rather than driving associative avoidance learning
description: The article proposes that parabrachial CGRP neurons regulate defensive behavioural output rather than serving as the obligatory aversive-US pathway for associative learning: in operant active avoidance, "CGRP signalling contributes les s to the associative processes underlying S-R learning than to t he regulation of defensive beha- vioural output though downstream CeA-dependent circuits." Silencing CGRP reduced freezing and nocifensive reactivity and enabled avoidance under high threat, shifting behavioural output from passive freezing toward active avoidance.
requirements: The interpretation rests on the PBA paradigm isolating threat-driven avoidance without appetitive reinforcement, so that performance changes reflect defensive response selection rather than reward-related processes.
constraints: TetTox silencing remained in effect throughout both conditioning and retention testing, preventing clear attribution of the behavioural effects to acquisition, retention, or expression of active avoidance.
The account is specific to operant active avoidance and differs from CGRP's established role in supporting associative learning in Pavlovian fear conditioning.
target_learning_goals: defensive response selection between passive freezing and active avoidance
operant avoidance learning under varying threat intensity
key_sources: Hanny Hayeon Lee, Eul Han & Yong Sang Jo. (2026). CGRP inhibition in the PBN shifts defensive strategy from freezing to active avoidance in a platform-based active avoidance paradigm. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00453-3

article_title: Teaching English Tense and Aspect with the Help of Cognitive Grammar: An Empirical Study
citation: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak. (2010). Teaching English tense and aspect with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 365-400. http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Cognitive grammar account of the English present tense, progressive aspect and perfective/imperfective verbs
description: The article presents a CG framework in which verbs designate processes profiled through conceived time via sequential scanning, and "CG assumes the division of all verbs into perfective and imperfective ones" — perfectives denoting bounded, changing situations, imperfectives stable, unbounded, homogeneous and contractible ones. On this account "the English progressive is used with perfective verbs to make them imperfective": -ing homogenizes component relations and excludes endpoints, while be restores sequential scanning. The present tense prototypically indicates a full instantiation of the profiled process coinciding with speech time, explaining performative verbs' compatibility with the simple present.
requirements: Instruction drawing on this account must convey the perfective/imperfective distinction and the imperfectivizing function of the progressive, as the cognitive treatment did
constraints: The article's treatment excluded intermediate verb types such as stance verbs and atelic activities, and focused only on reference to situations at speech time
target_learners: Polish senior high school learners of English
target_learning_goals: explicit knowledge of the English present simple/progressive with stative and dynamic verbs
examples: The cognitive treatment taught the account through pictorial figures, e.g. the verb trust portrayed as homogeneous and contractible and the verb build as bounded, with the present tense depicted as a keyhole
key_sources: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak. (2010). Teaching English tense and aspect with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 365-400. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1136451

article_title: Teaching English Tense and Aspect with the Help of Cognitive Grammar: An Empirical Study
citation: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak. (2010). Teaching English tense and aspect with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 365-400. http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: CG-based pedagogical grammar descriptions characterized by meaningfulness, non-arbitrariness, precision and pictorial illustration
description: Comparing CG and traditional descriptions as sources of pedagogical rules (Table 1), the article states that "the first difference between the traditional and CG approaches to grammatical description is the insistence of the latter on the meaningfulness of grammar and its provision of detailed analyses of grammatical meanings". Further listed characteristics are conceptualization/construal, inclusion of pragmatic factors, motivated rather than arbitrary rules, little vagueness, no contradictions between rules, and frequent use of pictorial illustrations of meaning, which traditional accounts lack.
requirements: Descriptions must provide detailed semantic analyses of the targeted grammatical features and pictorial representations of their meanings
constraints: The article notes potential drawbacks of CG in pedagogy: weak motivation behind certain meanings/uses, novel terminology, and the high degree of abstractness of some concepts
target_learners: second/foreign language learners of English grammar
target_learning_goals: understanding of grammatical form-meaning relationships (tense and aspect)
examples: The paper's CG description section abounds in figures illustrating grammatical meanings (Figures 1-6), while the traditional description section contains no such illustrations
key_sources: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak. (2010). Teaching English tense and aspect with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 365-400. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1136451

article_title: Teaching the English Active and Passive Voice with the Help of Cognitive Grammar: An Empirical Study
citation: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak, Anna Mystkowska-Wiertelak. (2013). Teaching the English active and passive voice with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching 3 (4). http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Cognitive grammar characterization of the English active and passive voice via the reference point model
description: The article presents a simplified CG account in which the subject is "a primary relational figure" and functions as a reference point establishing mental contact with the situation portrayed by the clause. Voice reflects "different configurations of salience": when focal prominence falls on the agent an active results; when topicality makes the patient more salient, a passive is used. Simplified versions of this characterization, with figures, formed the instructional treatment for the COG group.
requirements: Pedagogical use requires considerable simplification of the theory's abstract concepts, theory-specific terminology, and diagrammatic representations
constraints: The article identifies the theory's complexity and abstractness as a major potential drawback of CG as a basis for pedagogical grammar
target_learners: postpubescent EFL learners in a foreign language context
university BA students of elementary education
target_learning_goals: understanding the meaning and use of the English active and passive voice
form-meaning mappings for grammatical voice choice
examples: Figures 2, 3 and 4 illustrating Bell invented the telephone, The telephone was invented by Bell, and Our money was stolen were used in the COG treatment
key_sources: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak, Anna Mystkowska-Wiertelak. (2013). Teaching the English active and passive voice with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching 3 (4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135829

article_title: European training requirements in geriatric medicine 2025: driving competency-based education and harmonisation across Europe.
citation: Romero Ortuño R, van Iersel M, Nuotio MS, Kolk H, Topinková E, Schoevaerdts D, Farré Mercadé MV, Graf C, Cotobal Rodeles S, Vassallo MA, Vassallo M, Lütje D, Macijauskienė J, on behalf of the UEMS Geriatric Medicine Section (UEMS-GMS). (2026). European training requirements in geriatric medicine 2025: driving competency-based education and harmonisation across Europe. European Geriatric Medicine 17(2):417–428. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-025-01393-8
title: Build clinical EPAs around Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) as the core or stem
description: The article recommends that Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment, the defining hallmark of Geriatric Medicine, serve as the foundational "core or stem" from which most clinical EPAs branch out. CGA is a multidimensional, interdisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process with robust evidence for improving outcomes such as survival, recovery, and independence, and thus functions as both a clinical methodology and an educational framework. The committee reached consensus on this despite national differences in EPA implementation.
requirements: Trainers able to conduct and teach CGA across medical, psychological, functional and social domains
constraints: EPA implementation varies across European countries
target_learning_goals: competence in comprehensive geriatric assessment and integrated care planning
examples: Table 3 details the CGA EPA, mapping knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviours, assessment indicators such as the Mini-CEX and case-based discussions, and entrustment criteria
